issues.title: Enable support for typed `model_construct` besides mypy (incl. example implementation)
issues.body:
### Initial Checks - [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything - [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing ### Description Hi, guys! I really love pydantic, but there is the following issue that i really want to see resolved and i hope i can help: TL;DR: should `model_construct(...)` be typed (similar to `__init__`) and if so, what do you think about my solution of "copying" the `__init__` method signature? (If not, is there any official way of instantiating a model with type-checking but without validation?) Consider this simple model: ```python class User(BaseModel): id: int = Field(default_factory=lambda: randint(1, 1000)) name: str ``` If one wants to create model instances with data where the types are known at type-check time, they have to choose either `User(id=7, name="John Doe")` or `User.model_construct(id=7, name="John Doe")` The issue for me is, that the first option performs redundant (assuming type-checker correctness) validation at runtime and the second cannot perform any type-checks, because the signature is currently `model_construct(**kwargs: Any)`. According to your [docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/integrations/dev-tools/mypy/#generate-a-typed-signature-for-model_construct), the mypy plugin enables this behaviour for mypy, but a lot of users rely on other type-checking tools and it would be great if this functionality could be supported for them as well. Here is a simple (purely types-based) solution i came up with that seems to work for this use-case and i wanted to get some feedback before making it a proper MR. Essentially it simply copies the ParamSpec of the `__init__(...)` function into the `model_construct` method: ```python from typing_extensions import Protocol, TypeVar, ParamSpec, Callable, TYPE_CHECKING from pydantic import BaseModel P = ParamSpec("P") T = TypeVar("T") class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> Callable[P, T]: return owner class User(BaseModel): id: int = Field(default_factory=lambda: randint(1, 1000)) name: str if TYPE_CHECKING: @model_construct_decorator def model_construct_typed(self): ... else: @classmethod def model_construct_typed(cls, *args, **kwargs): return cls.model_construct(*args, **kwargs) User.model_construct_typed(id="7") # -> now also shows a type error in pyright ``` (The idea would be that what i currently named `model_construct_typed(...)` would be implemented as `model_construct(...)` on `BaseModel`) --- Now there are multiple solvable issues that ive left out for brevity, but here are their solutions for anyone interested:
1. What about the _fields_set argument of the current model_construct(...)? The `model_construct_decorator` can be updated as follows to reestablish that argument: ```python class ModelConstructCallable(Protocol[P, T]): def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T: ... class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> ModelConstructCallable[P, T]: return lambda _fields_set=None, *args, **kwargs: owner(*args, **kwargs) # could also be a simple pass statement with type-ignore comment, because this should never actually be executed ```
2. Will any of the current type-checking behaviour break? Since users currently have the `**kwarg` option available, this switch may break their existing code, especially if the pass `extra` data to model construct, as now their type-checker will complain about the extra data. There are two solutions for that issue: a) either keep the `model_construct(...)` as is and add a new `model_construct_typed(...)` b) add a new argument (e.g. `_type_check: bool=False`, after `_fields_set`) that optionally enables this behaviour Here is an example implementation of solution b) from a type-checking perspective (at runtime there should be no difference): ```python class ModelConstructCallable(Protocol[P, T]): @overload def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, _type_check: Literal[False]=False, **kwargs: Any) -> T: ... @overload def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, _type_check: Literal[True], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T: ... class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> ModelConstructCallable[P, T]: return lambda _fields_set=None, _type_check=False, *args, **kwargs: owner(*args, **kwargs) # could also be a simple pass statement with type-ignore comment, because this should never actually be executed ... User.model_construct(id="7", some_extra_value=...) # still no type error as before User.model_construct(_type_check=True, id="7", some_extra_value="...") # type error as intended ```
3. What about the instance version of the current model_construct(...)? I am not 100% sure what the behaviour is supposed to be when calling `model_construct(...)` on an instance of `BaseModel`, but i assume that it acts as a `classmethod`, so it should be the exact same method both on class- and instance-level. If thats the case, then the `model_construct_decorator` can be updated as follows to let type-checkers know that this is a valid use-case as well: ``` class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: Any, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> Callable[P, T]: # `instance: None` -> `instance: Any` stops type-checking errors when calling `User(...).model_construct_typed(...)` return owner ```
4. What about the current mypy plugin? and What about type-checker compatibility? The proposed solution is solely based on typing concepts and as such, any fully-fledged type-checker should be able to infer the data correctly. That being said, `mypy` does not have this capability (yet?), so the mypy plugin would still be required. Beyond that, i did initial tests of the change and here is the compatibility with common type checkers: | | mypy (no plugin)¹ | mypy (with plugin)¹ | pyright | ty | basedpyright | pyrefly | |-------------------------------|-------------------|--------------------|--------|----|--------------|--------| | `model_construct(...)` | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | | `model_construct_typed(...)` | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅⚠️² | ✅ | ❌ | (I couldnt get the legacy `pyre` working and `pytype` is outdated and also supports neither) ¹ Note that while using `model_construct_typed(...)` does not enable the desired functionality in mypy without plugin, it also does not break the existing functionality in mypy with plugin. ² Note that `ty` has some kind of builtin support for pydantic and internally replaces `id: int` with `id: LaxInt`, so this error would be caught `User.model_construct_typed(id=7)` (`name` argument missing), but this wouldnt `User.model_construct_typed(id="7", name="John Doe")`, because from the perspective of `ty`, `str` is assignable to `LaxInt`. An update from their side would be required, but i think it is a reasonable assumption that they would add support for that change. See [here](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/2403) for more info on the pydantic-in-ty support
--- Finally lets get to my main questions about all of this: - Is there general interest in this functionality or is it just me? If there is no interest, then how do you handle this use-case? - Are there any issues with my solutions that i have not addressed yet? - Is there anything else i should consider before starting on the actual implementation/MR? ### Affected Components - [ ] [Compatibility between releases](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/changelog/) - [x] [Data validation/parsing](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/#basic-model-usage) - [ ] [Data serialization](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/serialization/) - `.model_dump()` and `.model_dump_json()` - [ ] [JSON Schema](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/json_schema/) - [ ] [Dataclasses](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/dataclasses/) - [ ] [Model Config](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/config/) - [ ] [Field Types](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic/types/) - adding or changing a particular data type - [ ] [Function validation decorator](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/validation_decorator/) - [ ] [Generic Models](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/#generic-models) - [x] [Other Model behaviour](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/concepts/models/) - `model_construct()`, pickling, private attributes, ORM mode - [x] [Plugins](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/integrations/dev-tools/mypy/) and integration with other tools - mypy, FastAPI, python-devtools, Hypothesis, VS Code, PyCharm, etc.

issues.title: Type alias to `None` (or `MISSING`) not supported as a discriminated union member
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Using a `None` type alias as a member of a discriminated union fails during schema construction with `TypeError: The core schema type 'none' is not a valid discriminated union variant.`. The alias generates a `'none'` core schema reached through a `'definition-ref'`, and while `_handle_choice()` handles `'none'` choices (by wrapping the tagged union in a `'nullable'` schema), `_infer_discriminator_values_for_choice()` (which is what resolves `'definition-ref'` choices) doesn't.

Once https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13779 lands, the same applies to a type alias to the `MISSING` sentinel (a schema-less `'missing-sentinel'` schema reached through a `'definition-ref'`, see [this review comment](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13779#discussion_r3965416688)).

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Cat(BaseModel):
    kind: Literal['cat']


class Dog(BaseModel):
    kind: Literal['dog']


NoneAlias = TypeAliasType('NoneAlias', None)


class Model(BaseModel):
    pet: Annotated[NoneAlias | Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator='kind')] = None
#> TypeError: The core schema type 'none' is not a valid discriminated union variant.
```

issues.title: Concurrent TypeAdapter construction raises RuntimeError on free-threaded Python
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Constructing separate `TypeAdapter` instances concurrently for the same new `TypedDict` can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` on free-threaded Python.

A full run produced 91 failures in 800 attempts with the GIL disabled and none with `PYTHON_GIL=1`. It also reproduces on Pydantic main at `1c8a330acc3077e77da64e3672c7c875fb4c6eaa`.

Lazy annotation evaluation adds `__annotations_cache__` while another thread iterates `vars(typ).items()` in `_decorator_infos_for_class`.

### Example Code

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from typing_extensions import TypedDict


def run_round() -> None:
    class Record(TypedDict):
        value: int

    for index in range(1000):
        setattr(Record, f'metadata_{index}', index)

    barrier = threading.Barrier(8)

    def build(_: int) -> None:
        barrier.wait()
        TypeAdapter(Record).validate_python({'value': '42'})

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as executor:
        list(executor.map(build, range(8)))


for _ in range(100):
    run_round()
```

The synthetic attributes only widen the iteration window. They are not modified after the threads start.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
pydantic version: 2.13.5
pydantic-core version: 2.46.5
python version: 3.14.3 free-threading build
platform: macOS-26.6.2-arm64
related packages: typing_extensions-4.15.0
```

issues.title: `validate_call` cannot call a function with a keyword parameter named `self`
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ValidateCallWrapper.__call__` is declared as `def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs)`, so the instance is bound to the name `self`. A decorated function with a keyword parameter literally named `self` can then never be called with it: `f(self=1)` raises `TypeError: ValidateCallWrapper.__call__() got multiple values for argument 'self'` before validation runs. The wrapped function itself is fine with that name; it is only the wrapper's signature that collides. Same in 2.12.5, 2.13.5 and `pydantic/_internal/_validate_call.py` on main.

Making `self` positional-only in `__call__` (`def __call__(self, /, *args, **kwargs)`) removes the collision without changing anything else. Can send the PR.

### Example Code

```python
import pydantic.version
from pydantic import validate_call


@validate_call
def f(*, self: int) -> int:
    return self


try:
    print("f(self=1) ->", f(self=1))
except TypeError as e:
    print("f(self=1) -> TypeError:", e)
print(pydantic.version.version_info())
```

```
f(self=1) -> TypeError: ValidateCallWrapper.__call__() got multiple values for argument 'self'
```

issues.title: Pipeline API `multiple_of()` rejects every `timedelta` and raises `TypeError` for `date`/`time`/`datetime`
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In the pipeline API, `multiple_of()` is broken for every temporal type. `timedelta` rejects **every** value, including exact multiples, and `date`/`time`/`datetime` raise a bare `TypeError` that escapes as-is instead of a `ValidationError`.

| annotation | `.multiple_of(...)` | `Field(multiple_of=...)` | correct |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `float` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Decimal` | `multiple_of` error | `multiple_of` error | ✅ |
| `Fraction` | predicate check | n/a (unsupported by core) | ✅ |
| `timedelta` | **rejects everything** | accepts | ❌ |
| `date` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `time` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |
| `datetime` | **uncaught `TypeError`** | accepts | ❌ |

`validate_as(timedelta).multiple_of(timedelta(seconds=5))` rejects `timedelta(seconds=10)`, which is an exact multiple.

### Root cause

`_apply_constraint()` applies `multiple_of` natively only for a hardcoded `{'int', 'float', 'decimal'}`, and otherwise falls back to a Python predicate:

```python
def check_multiple_of(v: Any) -> bool:
    return v % multiple_of == 0
```

That predicate cannot work for temporal types:

* `timedelta(seconds=10) % timedelta(seconds=5)` is `timedelta(0)`, and `timedelta(0) == 0` is `False` in Python. The check therefore never holds, for any input.
* `date`, `time` and `datetime` do not support `%` at all, so the predicate raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %`, which is not wrapped into a `ValidationError`.

This looks like an oversight rather than a decision. #13659 generalised exactly this pattern for the other constraints, introducing `_ORDERING_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` and `_LENGTH_SCHEMA_TYPES` for `min_length`/`max_length`, both of which cover the temporal types. `MultipleOf` was left on its old hardcoded set in the same function.

Pydantic's own metadata already records the correct answer — `DATE_TIME_CONSTRAINTS` in `_known_annotated_metadata.py` includes `NUMERIC_CONSTRAINTS`, i.e. `multiple_of`:

```python
>>> from pydantic._internal._known_annotated_metadata import CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS
>>> sorted(CONSTRAINTS_TO_ALLOWED_SCHEMAS['multiple_of'])
['date', 'datetime', 'decimal', 'float', 'int', 'time', 'timedelta']
```

`fraction` is correctly absent there, and must keep using the predicate path — `fraction_schema()` takes no `multiple_of` argument, and `Fraction` supports `%` correctly.

### Suggested fix

Apply the constraint natively for the schema types that accept it, mirroring #13659:

```python
# Core schema types with native support for the `multiple_of` constraint:
_MULTIPLE_OF_SCHEMA_TYPES = frozenset({'int', 'float', 'decimal', 'date', 'time', 'datetime', 'timedelta'})
```

This aligns the pipeline API with the non-experimental API, per the position in #13564 that the two should agree. Note that this makes `multiple_of` a silent no-op on temporal types, because `pydantic-core` accepts the key but does not enforce it there — which is exactly what `Field(multiple_of=...)` already does today. Enforcing it would be a `pydantic-core` change and a separate discussion; this issue is only about the pipeline API diverging from `Field()`.

I have a fix and regression tests ready (the tests fail without the fix and pass with it, and `pyright` stays at its existing baseline). Happy to open a PR if I could be assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

td = datetime.timedelta

# 1. timedelta: an exact multiple is rejected.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[td, validate_as(td).multiple_of(td(seconds=5))])
ta.validate_python(td(seconds=10))
# ValidationError: Value error, Expected % 0:00:05 == 0
# (timedelta(0) == 0 is False, so the predicate never holds)

# 2. date/time/datetime: raw TypeError, not a ValidationError.
ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[datetime.date, validate_as(datetime.date).multiple_of(2)])
ta.validate_python(datetime.date(2020, 1, 1))
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %: 'datetime.date' and 'int'
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
             pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=debug pgo=false
               python version: 3.13.15 (main, Sep  1 2026, 14:18:08) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
                     platform: Linux-7.0.0-31-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.43
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0

```

issues.title: Allow `exclude_if` to depend on the serialization context (callable with `info`, or a context marker)
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

**TL;DR**: `Field(exclude_if=...)` (added in 2.12, #12141) decides exclusion from the field
*value* alone. Some exclusion decisions depend on the *caller* instead — most notably: *omit
credential fields from every dump by default, include them only when persistence explicitly
opts in via `context`*. #12056 already sketches extending `exclude_if` with the serialization
context; this issue is a concrete, production-tested use case for that extension — and I would
happily try to implement it (including the `pydantic-core` side), in whichever shape you
prefer.

#### The use case

Models holding third-party credentials (`client_secret`, RSA keys, connection strings):

1. Every ordinary serialization — API response, log payload, anything fed to an LLM — must not
   contain these fields. Omitted entirely, not masked: nothing to leak, and nothing for an API
   client to echo back on `PUT`.
2. Exactly one caller (database persistence) needs the real values through the same
   `model_dump` path, and opts in explicitly:
   `model_dump(context={'include_secrets': True})`.

This is, in essence, the user-defined ser/val modes idea (`'api'` vs `'dump-to-db'`) floated
in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/12056#issuecomment-3191434441 — expressed with
the `context` mechanism that exists today.

#### Why the current tools don't cover it

- `Field(exclude=True)` — unconditional; persistence cannot opt back in.
- `Field(exclude_if=...)` — the callable receives only the value, and the decision here
  depends on the caller, not on the value. Trying to accept `info` fails:

  ```python
  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

  class Model(BaseModel):
      api_key: str = Field(exclude_if=lambda value, info: True)

  Model(api_key='k').model_dump()
  #> TypeError: Model.<lambda>() missing 1 required positional argument: 'info'
  ```

- `SecretStr` / `Secret[T]` — masks instead of omitting (the key stays in the output), changes
  the runtime type of the field (`.get_secret_value()` at every read), and doesn't round-trip
  for non-str types. This is in fact what I was asking for back in #9827 (2024) — *"when
  fields are secret, we don't need them dumped and don't care about them"* — and the pattern
  below is what we eventually built while that issue stayed open. Full omission turned out to
  be the right semantics, not masking.
- `model_dump(exclude={...})` at each call site — one forgotten call site is a leak.
- A wrap `@model_serializer` reading `info.context` — this works and is what we run today, but
  it is surprisingly hard to keep the JSON schema intact around it (below). Discussion #11519
  shows others hitting the same wall for PII masking: the `WrapSerializer` suggested there is
  field-level — it can replace the value, but the key always stays.

#### What we run today

A marker + a base model with a wrap serializer:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, SerializerFunctionWrapHandler, model_serializer
from pydantic_core.core_schema import SerializationInfo


class OmittedSecret:
    pass


class SecretRemovingModel(BaseModel):
    @model_serializer(mode='wrap')
    def _strip_omitted_secret_fields(
        self, handler: SerializerFunctionWrapHandler, info: SerializationInfo
    ):
        data = handler(self)
        if isinstance(info.context, dict) and info.context.get('include_secrets'):
            return data
        for field_name, field_info in type(self).model_fields.items():
            if any(isinstance(meta, OmittedSecret) for meta in field_info.metadata):
                data.pop(field_name, None)
        return data


class ConnectionConfig(SecretRemovingModel):
    name: str
    client_secret: Annotated[str | None, OmittedSecret()] = None


config = ConnectionConfig(name='jira', client_secret='s3cr3t')
print(config.model_dump())
#> {'name': 'jira'}
print(config.model_dump(context={'include_secrets': True}))
#> {'name': 'jira', 'client_secret': 's3cr3t'}
```

We have been running this in production for over a year across two codebases and it works
well, but it carries real footguns a first-class mechanism would remove:

1. **The wrap serializer's return annotation silently destroys the schema.** Annotate it
   `-> dict[str, Any]` (as any typed codebase would) and every subclass's serialization schema
   collapses to a free-form object — with FastAPI, the entire typed response contract becomes
   `{[key: string]: unknown}`:

   ```python
   class Demo(SecretRemovingModel):  # with `-> dict[str, Any]` on the serializer
       name: str

   Demo.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')
   #> {'additionalProperties': True, 'type': 'object'}
   ```

   So the serializer must stay unannotated, the type checker silenced — and on top of that we
   maintain a hand-written `__get_pydantic_json_schema__` override on the base model to keep
   the published OpenAPI contract consistent with what the serializer actually emits.
2. **The whole model dump goes through a Python wrap serializer** — even models where only one
   of twenty fields is secret pay for it, and nested `SecretRemovingModel`s pay per level.
3. **Every model must inherit the base class** — a plain `BaseModel` with the marker silently
   does nothing.

Note that the JSON schema side of `exclude_if` is already exactly right for this use case:
since #12430, such fields stay in the serialization schema but are not `required` — which is
the correct static description of a field that may or may not be present depending on the
context.

#### Proposal

Either of the two shapes already floated in #12056 would cover this — I would happily try to
implement whichever you prefer, including the `pydantic-core` side:

1. **Let the `exclude_if` callable optionally receive `SerializationInfo`**, with the same
   signature inspection used for functional serializers (`info_arg` already exists in
   `pydantic-core`'s field schema machinery, so this is mostly plumbing):

   ```python
   def omit_secret(value: Any, info: SerializationInfo) -> bool:
       return not (isinstance(info.context, dict) and info.context.get('include_secrets'))


   class ConnectionConfig(BaseModel):
       name: str
       client_secret: Annotated[str | None, Field(exclude_if=omit_secret)] = None
   ```

2. **The marker API** — which I understand you may prefer to avoid a Python call on the hot
   path. I would happily try to implement the markers you consider right; the one my use case
   needs is a context-flag check, something like:

   ```python
   class ConnectionConfig(BaseModel):
       name: str
       client_secret: Annotated[str | None, Field(exclude_if=~ContextFlag('include_secrets'))] = None
   ```

   i.e. *"exclude unless the context flag is truthy"* — evaluated natively by `pydantic-core`
   with no Python call. Exact naming/composition (negation, `ContextIs(key, value)`, ...) is
   entirely up to you.

Which shape would you accept a PR for?

---

*Disclosure: this issue was drafted with the help of Claude (Fable 5, Anthropic) — for
structure and wording. I have verified every claim and every code sample myself (all outputs
above are from real runs on `pydantic==2.13.5`) and stand behind each word.*

### Affected Components

### Description

`re.Pattern` is serialized as its pattern string in JSON mode, so flags of a compiled regex are lost during serialization.

```text
    -> "abc"
    -> re.compile("abc")
```

I understand that serializing `re.Pattern` as a string is the documented behavior, but this makes JSON serialization lossy for patterns with flags.

issues.title: InstanceOf is callable at runtime but typed as non-callable, preventing runtime annotation introspection
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`InstanceOf[T]` works correctly as a model annotation, but the runtime `InstanceOf` marker cannot be constructed without a type-checking error.

Pydantic intentionally defines `InstanceOf` as `Annotated[AnyType, ...]` under `TYPE_CHECKING`, while exposing a callable dataclass at runtime. This allows type checkers to treat `InstanceOf[T]` as `T`, but means valid runtime introspection code sees `InstanceOf` as a non-callable `GenericAlias`.

Runtime annotation introspection is useful for libraries that inspect `BaseModel` fields to enforce policies, generate schemas, or distinguish special pydantic annotations from ordinary types. For example, we need to recognize `InstanceOf` to avoid recursively applying rules intended for the underlying type.

The current workaround is a targeted type-checker ignore:
```python
if InstanceOf() in get_args(annotation):  # ty: ignore[call-non-callable]
    ...
```

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import get_args, get_type_hints
from pydantic import BaseModel, InstanceOf

class Plugin:
    pass

class Model(BaseModel):
    plugin: InstanceOf[Plugin]

annotation = get_type_hints(Model, include_extras=True)["plugin"]
# Runtime result: `Annotated[Plugin, InstanceOf()]`

# The following line causes error when type-checked. E.g. for ty:
# error[call-non-callable]: Object of type `GenericAlias` is not callable
assert InstanceOf() in get_args(annotation)
```

issues.title: `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` on `Decimal` are missing from the JSON Schema for string values
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

For a constrained `Decimal` field, the numeric bound keywords only land on the `number` branch of the validation schema's `anyOf`. The `string` branch (which is how decimals arrive in JSON payloads, and how pydantic itself serializes them) has no bound information in either mode:

- Validation: `'0.5'` passes the schema (string branch, no bounds) but `gt=Decimal('1')` rejects it.
- Serialization: the schema is `{'type': 'string', 'pattern': ...}`, with no bound information, even though `model_dump_json()` always emits decimals as strings.

I'd expect the bound to reach string values too, or at least not be silently absent from the serialization schema. Right now, any consumer validating payloads against the generated schema (OpenAPI gateways, `jsonschema`, codegen validators) accepts values the model rejects. I hit this while validating API payloads against generated schemas in a data pipeline.

This also holds with the opt-in pattern from #13672: removing the pattern by default leaves the string branch without bounds in validation mode, and the serialization schema with none at all. The schema structure dates back to #11987 (2.12).

One possible direction: `build_decimal_pattern()` from #13672 already encodes `max_digits`/`decimal_places` best-effort in plain notation, and documents why exponents can't be constrained in a regex. The same approach could encode `gt`/`ge`/`lt`/`le` for plain-notation decimals, using the existing `_int_range_pattern` machinery, with the same exponent caveat.

Happy to work on this if someone assigns it to me.

### Example Code

```Python
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated

import jsonschema
from pydantic import Field, TypeAdapter

ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[Decimal, Field(gt=Decimal('1'))])

print(ta.json_schema(mode='validation'))
# {'anyOf': [{'exclusiveMinimum': 1.0, 'type': 'number'},
#            {'pattern': '^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$', 'type': 'string'}]}

print(ta.json_schema(mode='serialization'))
# {'pattern': '^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$', 'type': 'string'}  # no bounds at all

jsonschema.validate('0.5', ta.json_schema(mode='validation'))  # accepted
ta.validate_python('0.5')  # ValidationError: Input should be greater than 1
```

issues.title: Use `contentEncoding` and `contentMediaType` instead of `"format": "binary"` for `bytes` JSON Schema
issues.body:
Using `"format": "binary"` for the JSON Schema of `bytes` comes from OpenAPI 3.0.x: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.0.3.html#considerations-for-file-uploads.

Instead, we should make use of `contentEncoding` and `contentMediaType` (https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/draft-bhutton-json-schema-validation-01#section-8.3).

As `bytes` is a really common type, changing this in V2 would be quite disruptive.

See https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12841. Rebased branch: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/tree/vp/bytes-contentencoding.

issues.title: Serializing `mock.call` objects raises an exception
issues.body:
Originally reported in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/issues/1866:

The following code triggers a `TypeError`.

```python
from unittest.mock import call
from pydantic_core import to_jsonable_python

# TypeError: '_Call' object cannot be converted to 'SchemaSerializer'
to_jsonable_python(call(1, 2, 3), fallback=lambda call: call.args)
```

We usually try very hard to avoid raising errors from serialization, this is also on a type inference pathway. I think it'd be reasonable to just hit `fallback` if the `__pydantic_serializer__` attribute is invalid (this is the root cause of the `TypeError`).

issues.title: Smart union selects the wrong model in JSON mode with a before validator
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Adding a no-op `mode='before'` model validator makes smart-union validation select a model with fewer matching fields for JSON input. The equivalent Python input selects the model with more matching fields.

The example below prints:

```text
Larger
Smaller
```

I expect `Larger` in both cases: it has three supplied valid fields, while `Smaller` has two. This follows the documented [number-of-valid-fields-set ranking](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/unions/#number-of-valid-fields-set).

Reproduced on `main` at 965c23dd93bd5ca7b86224ba39ccbe79399f117b. In [model_fields.rs](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/965c23dd93bd5ca7b86224ba39ccbe79399f117b/pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), the Python-input helper adds its known-field count, then the outer validator adds `fields_set.len()` again. The before validator sends the smaller model through that Python-input path, while the larger model uses the plain JSON path and receives only the outer count.

I can send a focused fix with regression tests. Could you assign this to me?

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, model_validator


class Smaller(BaseModel):
    a: int
    b: int

    @model_validator(mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def keep_input(cls, value: Any) -> Any:
        return value


class Larger(BaseModel):
    a: int
    b: int
    c: int


adapter = TypeAdapter(Smaller | Larger)
print(type(adapter.validate_python({'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3})).__name__)
print(type(adapter.validate_json('{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}')).__name__)
```

issues.title: validate_by_alias=False still produces a validation JSON schema keyed by the alias
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

With `validate_by_alias=False`, the validation JSON schema still names the alias — which is the one key the model refuses.

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False, validate_by_name=True)
    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')

Model.model_json_schema()
#> {'properties': {'myAlias': ...}, 'required': ['myAlias'], ...}

Model(my_field='x')                          # accepted
Model.model_validate({'myAlias': 'x'})       # ValidationError
```

So the schema describes the opposite of the model: it requires the rejected key and omits the accepted one. `model_json_schema(by_alias=False)` produces the right document, but a caller has to know the model's config to know to ask for it.

### Why this looks like an oversight rather than a decision

`_get_alias_name` already picks the alias per mode, and it already returns the field name when no alias applies in that mode:

```python
elif self.mode == 'validation':
    alias = field.get('validation_alias', name)
else:
    alias = field.get('serialization_alias', name)
```

Which is visible in behaviour today:

| field | validation schema | serialization schema |
|---|---|---|
| `Field(serialization_alias='sAlias')` | `my_field` ✅ | `sAlias` ✅ |
| `Field(validation_alias='vAlias')` | `vAlias` ✅ | `my_field` ✅ |
| `Field(alias='myAlias')` + `validate_by_alias=False` | `myAlias` ❌ | `myAlias` |

The principle "use the alias only in the mode where it applies" is already implemented. `validate_by_alias=False` turns the validation alias off, and the generator simply does not consult it.

I have a fix and regression tests ready, and will open a PR without a closing reference so it does not trip `enforce-issue-assignment`.

### A related asymmetry I did not touch, because it is your call

`serialize_by_alias` defaults to `False`, so with nothing but a plain `Field(alias=...)` the serialization schema already disagrees with the default dump:

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')

Model(myAlias='x').model_dump_json()
#> {"my_field":"x"}

Model.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties']
#> {'myAlias': ...}
```

By the argument above that is the same defect. But unlike `validate_by_alias=False`, which is an explicit opt-out affecting only the people who set it, `serialize_by_alias=False` is the default, so honouring it would change the serialization schema of **every** aliased model. That is a breaking change and a product decision, not a drive-by fix, so I have deliberately left it alone and am raising it here instead. Happy to follow up either way you decide.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError


class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False, validate_by_name=True)

    my_field: str = Field(alias='myAlias')


print(list(Model.model_json_schema()['properties']))
#> ['myAlias']

print(Model(my_field='x'))
#> my_field='x'

try:
    Model.model_validate({'myAlias': 'x'})
except ValidationError as exc:
    print(exc.errors()[0]['type'])
    #> missing
```

issues.title: str_min_length and str_max_length are enforced by the validator but absent from the JSON schema
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`str_min_length` and `str_max_length` are enforced by the validator but do not appear in the JSON schema, so a JSON Schema validator silently accepts input the model rejects.

```python
class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(str_min_length=3)
    s: str

Model.model_json_schema()['properties']['s']
#> {'title': 'S', 'type': 'string'}       <-- no minLength

Model(s='ab')                             #> ValidationError
jsonschema.validate({'s': 'ab'}, Model.model_json_schema())   #> accepted
```

The same holds for `str_max_length`. This is the same class of defect as #13704 — a constraint pydantic applies that a consumer of the schema cannot see — but it comes from a different place, so that fix will not cover it.

### Why it happens

A field-level constraint lands on the core schema, where `GenerateJsonSchema.str_schema` finds it:

```python
'schema': {'type': 'str', 'min_length': 3}
```

A config-level one does not. It stays in the model's `config` block and is applied by pydantic-core at validation time, leaving the string node bare:

```python
{'type': 'model',
 'schema': {'type': 'model-fields',
            'fields': {'s': {'type': 'model-field', 'schema': {'type': 'str'}}}},   # <-- nothing here
 'config': {'str_min_length': 3, 'title': 'Model'}}
```

`str_schema` only reads the core schema node, so the constraint is invisible to it.

### Precedence

Worth stating because it decides what the schema should say when both are present: a field-level length **replaces** the config one rather than narrowing it. Measured on `main` (`952c239`):

| config | field | rejected lengths | schema today |
|---|---|---|---|
| `str_max_length=5` | — | 8, 12 | `{}` — nothing emitted |
| — | `max_length=10` | 12 | `maxLength: 10` ✅ |
| `str_max_length=5` | `max_length=10` | 12 | `maxLength: 10` ✅ |
| `str_max_length=10` | `max_length=5` | 8, 12 | `maxLength: 5` ✅ |
| `str_min_length=3` | — | 1 | `{}` — nothing emitted |
| `str_min_length=3` | `min_length=1` | none | `minLength: 1` ✅ |

So only the config-only rows are wrong, and the fix is to fall back to the config value when the field left the key unset — the rows that already work keep working untouched.

`str_strip_whitespace`, `str_to_lower` and `str_to_upper` are not affected: they transform rather than constrain, and the result is still a string, so the schema stays accurate.

### Example Code

```Python
import jsonschema
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError


class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(str_min_length=3, str_max_length=5)

    s: str


schema = Model.model_json_schema()
print(schema['properties']['s'])
#> {'title': 'S', 'type': 'string'}

for value in ('ab', 'abcdef'):
    try:
        Model(s=value)
    except ValidationError:
        print(f'pydantic rejects {value!r}')
    jsonschema.validate({'s': value}, schema)
    print(f'jsonschema accepts {value!r} -- constraint lost')
```

issues.title: Length constraints on deque, Counter and OrderedDict emit the string JSON Schema keywords (minLength) instead of minItems/minProperties
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`min_length`/`max_length` on a `deque` field produce `minLength`/`maxLength` in the JSON schema, on a schema of `"type": "array"`. On `Counter` and `OrderedDict` they produce the same string keywords on a schema of `"type": "object"`. Neither keyword applies to those types, so a JSON Schema validator ignores the constraint entirely:

```python
schema:     {'items': {'type': 'integer'}, 'minLength': 2, 'title': 'Items', 'type': 'array'}
pydantic:   rejected, as expected
jsonschema: ACCEPTED -- constraint silently lost
```

Every other container gets it right, which is what makes this look like an oversight rather than a decision:

| annotation | `"type"` | keyword emitted | correct |
|---|---|---|---|
| `list[int]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `set[int]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `frozenset[int]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `tuple[int, ...]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `Sequence[int]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `Iterable[int]` | array | `minItems` | ✅ |
| `deque[int]` | array | `minLength` | ❌ |
| `dict[str, int]` | object | `minProperties` | ✅ |
| `Counter[str]` | object | `minLength` | ❌ |
| `OrderedDict[str, int]` | object | `minLength` | ❌ |
| `str` / `bytes` | string | `minLength` | ✅ |

This is the same defect as #9256, which was reported for `Sequence` and fixed by #9303. That fix was narrow: `_known_annotated_metadata.py` picks the keyword by unwrapping `function-before`/`function-wrap`/`function-after` and then testing for a bare `list` schema, or a `json-or-python` wrapping one — the shape `Sequence` produces.

The three remaining types sit behind a wrapper the loop does not unwrap:

- `deque[int]` → `lax-or-strict` → `function-wrap` → `list`
- `Counter[str]` → `lax-or-strict` → `function-after` → `dict`
- `OrderedDict[str, int]` → `lax-or-strict` → `function-after` → `dict`

So they fall through to the `else` branch and get the string keywords. The `dict` case also shows the mapping needs a third answer (`minProperties`/`maxProperties`), not just the two the current code chooses between.

I have a fix and regression tests ready — happy to open a PR if someone assigns this to me.

### Example Code

```Python
from collections import Counter, OrderedDict, deque
from typing import Annotated

import jsonschema
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter, ValidationError


class M(BaseModel):
    items: deque[int] = Field(min_length=2)


schema = M.model_json_schema()
print(schema['properties']['items'])
# {'items': {'type': 'integer'}, 'minLength': 2, 'title': 'Items', 'type': 'array'}

payload = {'items': [1]}  # one element, violates min_length=2

try:
    M.model_validate(payload)
except ValidationError:
    print('pydantic: rejected, as expected')

jsonschema.validate(payload, schema)
print('jsonschema: ACCEPTED -- constraint silently lost')

# mappings, for comparison
for name, ann in [
    ('dict', dict[str, int]),
    ('Counter', Counter[str]),
    ('OrderedDict', OrderedDict[str, int]),
]:
    print(name, TypeAdapter(Annotated[ann, Field(min_length=1)]).json_schema())
# dict        {'additionalProperties': ..., 'minProperties': 1, 'type': 'object'}
# Counter     {'additionalProperties': ..., 'minLength': 1, 'type': 'object'}
# OrderedDict {'additionalProperties': ..., 'minLength': 1, 'type': 'object'}
```

issues.title: Support gt/ge/lt/le sign constraints for `Decimal` JSON Schema pattern
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

For Decimal fields with a sign-determining constraint (positive-only, negative-only), the generated JSON Schema Regex pattern still allows both signs, even though the field can never validate a value of the excluded sign.

Pydantic-core itself validates correctly (a negative string is rejected by the gt=0 check at runtime), so this isn't a validation bypass in normal use. However, the pattern and the minimum in the schema are inconsistent, which can cause problems for:
- OpenAPI client codegen tools that only look at pattern
- Client-side form validators (e.g. Swagger UI) that check pattern but not minimum/exclusiveMinimum

I've specifically encountered this as an issue in the context of using Schemathesis to fuzz my FastAPI implementation.

## Proposed fix:
When the constraint restricts valid values to a single sign (positive or negative), restrict the sign character class accordingly:
    ge=x or gt=x where x >= 0→ [+-]? becomes [+]?  
    le=y or lt=y where y is < 0 → [+-]? becomes [-]?

I am not trying to make the regex pattern enforce specific numeric bounds. For example, if the constraint "ge=5" is used, the regex pattern may still result in an invalid value such as "4.2". However, I believe the use-case where ge/gt=0 is common enough that this would make a meaningful correctness improvement without introducing significant complexity. Below is my proposed approach to implementing this change (not yet tested):
```
def get_decimal_pattern(schema: core_schema.DecimalSchema) -> str:
    max_digits = schema.get('max_digits')
    decimal_places = schema.get('decimal_places')

    ge = schema.get('ge')
    gt = schema.get('gt')
    le = schema.get('le')
    lt = schema.get('lt')

    # Determine the permitted sign based on the numeric constraints.
    if (ge is not None and ge >= 0) or (gt is not None and gt >= 0):
        sign_pattern = r'[+]?'
    elif (le is not None and le < 0) or (lt is not None and lt < 0):
        sign_pattern = r'[-]?'
    else:
        sign_pattern = r'[+-]?'

    pattern = (
        rf'^(?!^[-+.]*$){sign_pattern}0*'
        # check it is not empty string and not one or sequence of ".+-" characters.
    )...
```

This would build on max_digits and decimal_places from #11987 without changing the API. 

### Example Code

```Python
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Item(BaseModel):
    quantity: Annotated[Decimal, Field(gt=0)]

print(Item.model_json_schema())
# {'properties': {'qty': {'anyOf': [{'exclusiveMinimum': 0.0, 'type': 'number'}, {'pattern': '^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$', 'type': 'string'}], 'title': 'Qty'}}, 'required': ['qty'], 'title': 'Item', 'type': 'object'}
```

issues.title: model_dump_json crashes on a SecretStr field with an unvalidated None default (internal AttributeError instead of null/warning)
issues.body:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed the bug exists on the latest version of pydantic (2.13.4) and on current `main`.

### Python Version

3.13.14

### Pydantic Version

pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core (latest from pip at time of report)

### Description

A model field annotated `SecretStr` with an **unvalidated `None` default** crashes serialization to JSON. Per [models docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/), field defaults are only validated when `validate_default=True`, so constructing such a model without arguments is legal — and every other scalar annotation serializes the unvalidated default as `null`. For `SecretStr`, however, `model_dump_json()` raises instead.

Note this is specific to the JSON path and to the *non-nullable* annotation:
* `model_dump()` (python mode) returns `None` fine;
* `Optional[SecretStr] = None` dumps to JSON correctly (`{"s":null}`);
* a control field `n: int = None` also dumps fine — so only the combination "non-nullable SecretStr + None default + JSON serializer" hits the broken path.

### Example Code

```python
import warnings
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr

class M(BaseModel):
    n: int = None          # same pattern, control group
    s: SecretStr = None    # crashes

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    print(M().model_dump())          # {'n': None, 's': None}  -- OK
    try:
        print(M().model_dump_json())
    except Exception as e:
        print(type(e).__name__, "|", e)
    print("warnings emitted:", len(w))

class O(BaseModel):
    s: Optional[SecretStr] = None

print(O().model_dump_json())         # {"s":null} -- OK
```

### Actual behavior

```
{'n': None, 's': None}
PydanticSerializationError | Error calling function '_serialize_secret_field': AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get_secret_value'
warnings emitted: 0
{"s":null}
```

The exception escapes even though the value mismatch is exactly the situation the serialization layer normally degrades gracefully on (serialize as-is / warn). No `UserWarning` about the mismatched default is emitted either.

Looking at `_serialize_secret_field`, it calls `.get_secret_value()` unconditionally when the serializer runs with `when_used='always'`; there is no guard for `value is None` on a non-optional annotation, while core handles `None` defaults for other types before user serializers are reached.

### Expected behavior

Either of the consistent-with-everything-else outcomes:

1. serialize the unvalidated default as `null`: `{"n":null,"s":null}` (matching how `int = None`, `str = None` etc. behave), or
2. at minimum emit the standard serialization-mismatch `UserWarning` instead of raising an internal `AttributeError` wrapped into `PydanticSerializationError`.

The current traceback points users at pydantic internals rather than their own model definition.

issues.title: `populate_by_name` (and implicit `validate_by_name` when `validate_by_alias=False`) is ignored by `@validate_call`
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Since v2.11, `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True))` no longer allows passing an aliased parameter by its name — the same config on a `BaseModel` works, and the [`populate_by_name` docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.populate_by_name) say it is strictly equivalent to `validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True` (deprecated in v3, but still supported). Works on 2.10.6; broken on 2.11.x, 2.12.x, and `main`.

A worse variant: `@validate_call(config=ConfigDict(validate_by_alias=False))` makes the aliased parameter impossible to provide at all (both name and alias raise), even though #11503 made `validate_by_alias=False` implicitly enable `validate_by_name`.

Root cause: `_arguments_schema()`/`_arguments_v3_schema()` embed `validate_by_name=self._config_wrapper.validate_by_name` into the core schema (`_generate_schema.py:2081/2149`), reading the raw config key. The backwards-compatibility patch mapping `populate_by_name` → `validate_by_name` only runs inside `ConfigWrapper.core_config()`, and pydantic-core gives the schema-embedded value precedence over the validator config, so the patched core config is never consulted. Models are unaffected because model-fields schemas don't embed the flag.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, validate_call

@validate_call(config=dict(populate_by_name=True))
def f(a: Annotated[int, Field(alias='b')]) -> int:
    return a

f(b=1)  # OK
f(a=1)  # ValidationError: Unexpected keyword argument
```

issues.title: Change `NameEmail` validation behavior
issues.body:
The [`NameEmail`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic/networks/#pydantic.networks.NameEmail) type currently uses a regex implementation to validate input:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/2151025aa51263f3016502b00010b78e4481eaa1/pydantic/networks.py#L1310-L1318

But I'm not sure the pattern is really correct:

1. Other regex patterns online are quite different (https://gist.github.com/gregseth/5582254, https://regexr.com/2rhq7, https://regex101.com/library/3uvtNl)
2. I'm not sure it complies fully to the [RFC 5322](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322#section-3.4)

One option could be to use the stdlib directly (e.g. [`email.utils.parseaddr()`](https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/email.utils.html#email.utils.parseaddr)). However, behavior can change between Python versions (similar problems to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13587#issuecomment-5190537146). There's also the private [`email._header_value_parser`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/20e6c2fc7c174342214d561845419c4030f8638f/Lib/email/_header_value_parser.py) module, which seems to be properly compliant with RFC 5322.

issues.title: Independently rebuild nested models when used within other core schema generation contexts
issues.body:
https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/11388 refactored how fields (in particular incomplete fields) were handled during core schema generation. It fixed a class of issues where `FieldInfo` instances of a model referenced by another model were wrongly mutated:

```python
class Sub(BaseModel):
    f: 'Forward'

# Sub.f is incomplete

class Main(BaseModel):
    sub: Sub

# When building `Main`, building field `sub` would mutate the `FieldInfo` instance
# of `Sub.f`, leading to all kind of issues.

# Sub.f is complete
```

This is no longer the case today. When encountering an incomplete sub model (e.g. `Sub` in our example), we independently re-collect model fields without altering anything on `Sub`:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/59af43ad35d6b69534e7d18230ee87189320bac4/pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py#L835-L862

And https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/11388 states:

> On important thing to acknowledge: when encountering `sub: Sub`, we don't call `Sub.model_rebuild()`. Doing so might be the right thing to do, but is unfortunately not backwards compatible. The reason is that the NS Resolver used for `Model` might contain annotations (e.g. provided through the [`parent_namespace`](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/929e8f47ede2f895290714a6de96e6fb7b4c926c/pydantic/_internal/_namespace_utils.py#L226)) that should be available for `Sub`. This means that even if `sub: Sub` successfully builds, `Sub` isn't complete yet — each model should be rebuilt independently, through `model_rebuild()`).

This backwards compatibility edge case is covered in this test:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/d6e2021f761fc6bd53bd955a9cc3916cc5d0bfe6/tests/test_forward_ref.py#L1196-L1224

However, this is a missed opportunity, in particular when using [`defer_build`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic/config/#pydantic.config.ConfigDict.defer_build). Most of the time, it is perfectly fine to have `Sub` being rebuilt, without risks of polluting namespace resolution:

```python
class Sub(BaseModel, defer_build=True):
    f: int

class Main1(BaseModel):
    sub: Sub

# At this point, Sub is still incomplete

class Main2(BaseModel):
    sub: Sub

# At this point, Sub is still incomplete too,
# and the building process of Sub was done twice
```

In particular, this means prebuilt validator/serializer reuse (introduced in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1616) wont work here. Measured on https://github.com/Kludex/httpx2-k8s, this goes from ~24MB to 5MB.

issues.title: Fields in multiple inheritance: base that only inherits a field shadows a later base's override (MRO not respected)
issues.body:
## Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

## Description

This is kin of #11700 (private attributes in multiple inheritance don't respect the MRO). That issue's example shows public fields resolving correctly when both bases declare the field. This report covers the shape that still diverges from the MRO: a base that *merely inherits* an attribute shadows a later base's override.

The same shape with plain Python classes resolves per the MRO, for both attribute kinds, in both base orders:

```python
class Base:
    f = "base"
    _knob = "base"

class Override(Base):
    f = "override"
    _knob = "override"

class Plain(Base):
    pass

class Swapped(Plain, Override):
    pass

class Composed(Override, Plain):
    pass

print(Swapped().f, Swapped()._knob)    # override override
print(Composed().f, Composed()._knob)  # override override
```

## Example Code

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Base(BaseModel):
    f: str = "base"
    _knob: str = "base"

class Override(Base):
    f: str = "override"
    _knob: str = "override"

class Plain(Base):
    pass

class Swapped(Plain, Override):
    pass

class Composed(Override, Plain):
    pass

print(Swapped.mro())  # [Swapped, Plain, Override, Base, BaseModel, object]
print(Swapped().f, Swapped()._knob)    # base override
print(Composed().f, Composed()._knob)  # override base
```

`Plain` never declares `f` or `_knob`; it only carries inherited copies in its flattened `__pydantic_fields__` and `__private_attributes__`.

| base order | field | private attr |
|---|---|---|
| `(Plain, Override)` | `"base"` ❌ | `"override"` ✅ |
| `(Override, Plain)` | `"override"` ✅ | `"base"` ❌ |

Native Python resolves `override override` for both attribute kinds in both orders. No ordering of the same two pydantic bases resolves both correctly. Each merge picks a winner from the declared bases in a fixed direction: fields take the first declared base whose flattened `__pydantic_fields__` contains the name (inherited copies included), private attributes take the last declared base. The two directions are opposite, so each rule is MRO-correct only in the shape where the other breaks. #11700's example happened to use the both-declare shape, where fields resolve correctly, which is likely why the field side went unnoticed.

## Cause as I read it

Inherited fields are merged from base snapshots in declared order, where the first declared base whose snapshot contains the name wins, inherited copies included. A base that merely inherits the field therefore occupies the winning slot over a later base's override. Merging in MRO order would fix this and #11700 together.

issues.title: JSON Schema ignores `ser_json_temporal`, so serialization schemas contradict `model_dump_json()` output
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`ser_json_temporal` landed in v2.12 and controls how `datetime`, `date`, `time` and `timedelta` are serialized to JSON. `GenerateJsonSchema` was never told about it, so a `mode='serialization'` schema still says these fields are strings even when `model_dump_json()` writes numbers.

With `ser_json_temporal='seconds'` (same with `'milliseconds'`), every temporal field is affected:

```
schema:  {'dt': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'date-time'}, 'td': {'type': 'string', 'format': 'duration'}}
dump:    {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'td': 86400.0}
```

Running that payload through a JSON Schema validator fails with `1577836800.0 is not of type 'string'`, so the schema pydantic publishes rejects the output pydantic itself just produced. `date_schema`, `time_schema` and `datetime_schema` read no config at all right now.

There is a second mismatch that goes the other way, on `timedelta`. `timedelta_schema` only looks at the older `ser_json_timedelta` setting. The docs for `ser_json_temporal` say it takes precedence over `ser_json_timedelta`, and pydantic-core implements exactly that: `SerializationConfig::from_config` and `TimeDeltaSerializer::build` both check whether `ser_json_temporal` is present in the config before falling back to `ser_json_timedelta`. The JSON schema layer does not, so setting `ser_json_temporal='iso8601'` together with `ser_json_timedelta='float'` gives you the reverse problem:

```
schema:  {'td': {'type': 'number'}}
dump:    {'td': 'P1D'}
```

For anyone generating an OpenAPI document from a model this is a silent wrong answer rather than a crash, which is probably why it has gone unnoticed since the setting was added.

I have a patch that mirrors the pydantic-core resolution in the four temporal schema methods, plus tests. Happy to open a PR if you want to assign this to me.

### Example Code

```Python
import json
from datetime import date, datetime, time, timedelta

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class Numeric(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='seconds')

    dt: datetime
    d: date
    t: time
    td: timedelta


model = Numeric(dt=datetime(2020, 1, 1), d=date(2020, 1, 1), t=time(12, 0), td=timedelta(days=1))

print(Numeric.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'dt': {'format': 'date-time', 'title': 'Dt', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'd': {'format': 'date', 'title': 'D', 'type': 'string'},
#>  't': {'format': 'time', 'title': 'T', 'type': 'string'},
#>  'td': {'format': 'duration', 'title': 'Td', 'type': 'string'}}

print(json.loads(model.model_dump_json()))
#> {'dt': 1577836800.0, 'd': 1577836800.0, 't': 43200.0, 'td': 86400.0}


# The timedelta precedence case, wrong in the opposite direction:
class Precedence(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(ser_json_temporal='iso8601', ser_json_timedelta='float')

    td: timedelta


print(Precedence.model_json_schema(mode='serialization')['properties'])
#> {'td': {'title': 'Td', 'type': 'number'}}

print(json.loads(Precedence(td=timedelta(days=1)).model_dump_json()))
#> {'td': 'P1D'}
```

issues.title: Runtime by_name/by_alias arguments dropped by model_validator(mode="wrap")
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The `handler` passed to a wrap-mode model validator appears to silently drop the passed-in `by_name`/`by_alias` arguments from the top-level `validate_python` methods.


### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Self
from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter, ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler, model_validator

CFG = {"alias_generator": lambda s: s.replace("_", "-"), "validate_by_name": True}

class Plain(BaseModel):
    model_config = CFG
    build_depends: list[str] = []

class Wrapped(BaseModel):
    model_config = CFG
    build_depends: list[str] = []

    @model_validator(mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def _noop(cls, data, handler: ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler) -> Self:
        return handler(data)

data = {"build_depends": ["x"]}  # field name, not the alias
print(TypeAdapter(Plain).validate_python(data, by_alias=True, by_name=False))    # build_depends=[]    correct
print(TypeAdapter(Wrapped).validate_python(data, by_alias=True, by_name=False))  # build_depends=['x'] wrong
```

issues.title: [Bug] Experimental pipeline .len() adds redundant Python-level validation for native length types
issues.body:
## Bug description

In Pydantic's experimental pipeline API, `.len()` appears to add a redundant Python-level length check even when the underlying type natively supports `min_length` / `max_length`.

For example:

```python
validate_as(str).len(2, 10)
```

produces a core schema equivalent to:

```text
function-after(check_len) wrapping str(min_length=2, max_length=10)
```

The native Pydantic validation already enforces the length constraints, but the additional Python-level `check_len` wrapper performs the same validation again.

This behavior is different from the other pipeline constraints such as `.gt()`, `.ge()`, `.lt()`, `.le()`, and `.multiple_of()`, which avoid adding an unnecessary Python-level wrapper when the underlying type supports the constraint natively.

## Expected behavior

When the underlying type natively supports length constraints, `.len()` should rely on the native `min_length` / `max_length` schema constraints without adding a redundant Python-level length check.

For types that do not natively support length constraints, the Python-level fallback should continue to be used.

## Reproduction

The issue can be observed by inspecting the generated core schema:

```python
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

schema = validate_as(str).len(2, 10)

print(schema._steps)
```

The resulting schema contains both the native string length constraint and an additional Python-level validation wrapper.

The same pattern occurs for other native length types such as:

- `str`
- `list`
- `tuple`
- `set`
- `frozenset`
- `dict`

## Proposed fix

The `Len` constraint handling in `_apply_constraint()` should mirror the structure used by the other constraints: apply the native constraint when supported and only use the Python-level fallback when native support is unavailable.

I have locally verified a minimal implementation of this approach and added regression coverage that checks the generated schema structure.

## Validation

The local regression test fails on the current unfixed implementation and passes with the proposed change.

The relevant pipeline test suite also passes.

## Contribution

I would like to work on this issue. If the proposed approach is acceptable, could you please assign the issue to me before I open a PR?

issues.title: `SerializeAsAny` fails on a deferred model: `TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'`
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Serialization with `SerializeAsAny` fails when the runtime class of the value is a deferred model.
A deferred model is a model with `defer_build=True` that pydantic did not build yet.
The call raises this error:

```
PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError: 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'
```

I expect pydantic to build the deferred model at first use, and then serialize the value.

### Cause

The cause is in pydantic-core, in `src/serializers/infer.rs`.
The function `serialize_pydantic_serializable` reads the attribute `__pydantic_serializer__` from the value.
On a deferred model, this attribute holds a `MockValSer` object, not a `SchemaSerializer` object.
The code downcasts the object to `SchemaSerializer`.
The downcast fails, and the error goes to the caller.

`MockValSer` has a lazy rebuild hook in `__getattr__`.
A Python method call starts this hook.
A Rust downcast does not start this hook.
As a result, the same deferred instance serializes correctly through a direct `model_dump_json()`, but fails through `SerializeAsAny`.
The example code below shows this asymmetry.

### Impact

This failure occurred for us in production.
A worker process serialized instances of model classes that it never validated in that process.
Each `model_dump_json()` call on the parent model failed.

### Versions tested

The failure occurs on all versions that we tested:

- pydantic 2.12.5 / pydantic-core 2.41.5
- pydantic 2.13.4 / pydantic-core 2.46.4
- pydantic 2.14.0b1 / pydantic-core 2.48.0

### Related issues

- #7713 tracks `MockValSer` errors in general.
- #12282 reported this failure and was closed as a duplicate.

### Proposed fix

I have a fix with tests ready on a fork.
The fix changes `get_pydantic_serializer` in `infer.rs`:

1. The function downcasts the attribute value to `SchemaSerializer` as before.
2. If the downcast fails, the function calls the `rebuild()` method of the mock object.
3. The function then uses the serializer that `rebuild()` returns.
4. An object without a `rebuild()` method keeps the current downcast error.

`serialize_pydantic_serializable` and `PolymorphismTrampoline` use the same code path, so one change repairs both.
All pydantic and pydantic-core test suites pass with the fix.
Please assign this issue to me, and I will open the pull request.


### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, SerializeAsAny


class Child(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)
    x: int = 1


class Sub(Child):
    y: int = 2


class Parent(BaseModel):
    content: Optional[SerializeAsAny[Child]] = None


# model_construct() does not validate, so pydantic does not build Sub.
# This is equal to a process that serializes a class that it never validated.
sub = Sub.model_construct(x=1, y=2)
parent = Parent.model_construct(content=sub)
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is False

# 1) The SerializeAsAny path fails on the deferred model.
try:
    parent.model_dump_json()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    # PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: TypeError:
    # 'MockValSer' object is not an instance of 'SchemaSerializer'

# 2) The direct Python path rebuilds the same deferred model and succeeds.
print(sub.model_dump_json())  # {"x":1,"y":2}
assert Sub.__pydantic_complete__ is True

# 3) After the rebuild, the SerializeAsAny path also succeeds.
print(parent.model_dump_json())  # {"content":{"x":1,"y":2}}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.14.0b1
        pydantic-core version: 2.48.0
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.15 (main, Mar 25 2026, 02:58:47) [Clang 22.1.1 ]
                     platform: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit
```

issues.title: TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' in match_type for PEP 695 aliases with a ParamSpec (regression in 2.14.0b1)
issues.body:
Reported downstream in Giskard-AI/giskard#2719 (breaks `import giskard.checks`); repro and analysis below. The report was drafted jointly with @davidberenstein1957, who invited it to be filed upstream as-is.

### Description

`_generate_schema.match_type` added an unguarded dict lookup in 2.14 that assumes the annotation object is hashable. It is not, for a PEP 695 type alias with a `ParamSpec` parameterized by an empty list. Schema building for any model containing such an annotation crashes.

This is a regression: the same code builds fine on 2.13.4.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel

type Alias[**P, R] = Any

class M(BaseModel):
    f: Alias[[], int] | None = None
```

Raises immediately at class-definition time:

```
File ".../pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py", line 1127, in match_type
    if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

### Mechanism

`Alias[[], int]` is a `types.GenericAlias` whose `__args__` is `([], int)`. Hashing the alias hashes that tuple, which contains a `list` — so it is unhashable. The line at `_generate_schema.py:1127`

```python
if origin is not None and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

calls `.get(obj)` without checking that `obj` can be hashed. `dict.get` propagates the `TypeError` rather than treating an unhashable key as absent.

### Suggested fix

Guard the lookup, e.g.

```python
if origin is not None and isinstance(obj, Hashable) and (aliased_obj := typing_objects.DEPRECATED_ALIASES.get(obj)):
```

or wrap it in `try/except TypeError`. An unhashable object cannot be a `DEPRECATED_ALIASES` key by construction, so skipping the lookup is always correct.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

- pydantic 2.14.0b1 (fails) / 2.13.4 (works)
- Python 3.12.13
- Reproduced on Linux and macOS

### Real-world impact

Hit in [giskard-oss](https://github.com/Giskard-AI/giskard-oss), where `type GeneratorType[**P, R, S] = ...` parameterized as `GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]` makes `import giskard.checks` fail outright under 2.14.0b1. Instrumenting `match_type` confirms the offending object:

```
OFFENDING obj  = GeneratorType[[], InputType, None]
OFFENDING type = <class 'types.GenericAlias'>
OFFENDING args = ([], InputType, None)
```

There is no workaround on the library side short of pinning `pydantic<2.14` (done in Giskard-AI/giskard#2752), which is what downstream has had to do.

issues.title: JSON schema discriminator mapping uses Python-style `True`/`False` keys for `bool` discriminators
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a discriminated union uses a `bool` discriminator (`Literal[True]` / `Literal[False]`), the generated JSON schema's `discriminator.mapping` uses the Python string representations `"True"` and `"False"` as keys:

```json
"discriminator": {
    "mapping": {"False": "#/$defs/Disabled", "True": "#/$defs/Enabled"},
    "propertyName": "enabled"
}
```

Per the [OpenAPI discriminator specification](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0#discriminator-object), mapping keys must match the serialized payload value of the discriminator property. For a boolean property, that value serializes to JSON `true`/`false`, so the keys should be `"true"` and `"false"`. Tooling that resolves the mapping against the payload (code generators, validators such as openapi-generator or Redocly) fails to match either variant.

Expected:

```json
"mapping": {"false": "#/$defs/Disabled", "true": "#/$defs/Enabled"}
```

Note that `Enum` discriminator keys are already normalized to their value (`k.value`) before stringification in `GenerateJsonSchema.tagged_union_schema`; `bool` keys just fall through to `str(k)`.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Enabled(BaseModel):
    enabled: Literal[True]
    config: str


class Disabled(BaseModel):
    enabled: Literal[False]


class Model(BaseModel):
    setting: Enabled | Disabled = Field(discriminator='enabled')


print(Model.model_json_schema()['properties']['setting']['discriminator'])
# {'propertyName': 'enabled', 'mapping': {'True': '#/$defs/Enabled', 'False': '#/$defs/Disabled'}}
```

issues.title: `Decimal` json schema pattern relies on look-around assertions
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In addition to the problems outlined in #13089, the pattern added in #11987 makes use of look-around assertions, which are not supported by all regex implementations, including the default implementation pydantic relies on. Which means pydantic will reject its own decimal pattern if used as an explicit `pattern` with the default backend.

If it is not possible to write an equivalent correct pattern without look-around assertions, at the very least there should be an option to avoid emitting regex patterns, that cannot be parsed by regex implementations that do not support lookahead/lookbehind assertions.

Although in this case I believe it should be very simple to not use a look-around assertion, by simply relying on `|` instead.

### Example Code

```Python
import re
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, RootModel
from typing import Annotated

class Foo(BaseModel):
    bar: Decimal

schema = Foo.model_json_schema()
RootModel[Annotated[str, Field(
    pattern=schema['properties']['bar']['anyOf'][1]['pattern']
)]].model_validate_json('1.4')
```

issues.title: Memory leak: transient models using Enum methods or Field(exclude_if=...) survive GC
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Transient `BaseModel` classes are not collected when either:
* A model field references an `Enum` whose class defines a Python method.
* A model field uses `Field(exclude_if=<Python callable>)`.

After the defining module is removed from `sys.modules` and every ordinary strong reference is dropped, weak references to the model and enum classes remain alive after repeated full `gc.collect()` calls. Repeating this construction in disposable module namespaces causes linear memory growth.

Controls using an enum without methods or a field without `exclude_if` are collected normally.

I encountered this in combination with a Temporal workflow sandbox. With a large interconnected model graph and high volume Temporal workflows this can result in multi-GiB process growth relatively quickly.

The likely cause is missing `PyGcTraverse` edges for Python objects held by pydantic-core:
* `SerField` owns `serialization_exclude_if`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/fields.rs#L26-L38
* `EnumSerializer` owns `class`, but traverses only `serializer`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/serializers/type_serializers/enum_.rs
* Each `EnumValidator<T>` owns `lookup`, but traverses only `class` and `missing`: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c/pydantic-core/src/validators/enum_.rs

Traversing `py_schema` does not compensate for another unreported direct reference: CPython’s collector accounts for every actual strong edge individually.

I tested a temporary build from Pydantic `main` at `c67a1397327c6abc1a2e2e921af01aebbbeedf1c`. Adding only these traversal edges made all objects in the reproduction collectible:
* Add `serialization_exclude_if` to `SerField` traversal.
* Add `class` to `EnumSerializer` traversal.
* Add `lookup` to every `EnumValidator<T>` traversal.

For the enum case, changing only the serializer or only the validator was insufficient; both missing edges were required.

This appears related to earlier missing-traversal fixes such as:

* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5136
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/787
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1100

I would be happy to submit a focused patch.

(please note that this analysis was LLM assisted)

### Example Code

```Python
import gc
import sys
import types
import weakref

def transient_module(name, source, class_names):
    module = types.ModuleType(name)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    exec(compile(source, f"<{name}>", "exec"), module.__dict__)
    refs = tuple(
        weakref.ref(module.__dict__[class_name])
        for class_name in class_names
    )
    del sys.modules[name]
    del module
    return refs

enum_ref, enum_model_ref = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_enum_gc_repro",
    """
from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Membership(str, Enum):
    FULL = "full"
    def label(self) -> str:
        return self.value
class Model(BaseModel):
    membership: Membership
""",
    ("Membership", "Model"),
)

(exclude_if_model_ref,) = transient_module(
    "_pydantic_exclude_if_gc_repro",
    """
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class Model(BaseModel):
    value: int = Field(exclude_if=lambda value: False)
""",
    ("Model",),
)

for _ in range(5):
    gc.collect()

# All three should be False because no intentional strong references remain.
print("enum alive:", enum_ref() is not None)
print("enum model alive:", enum_model_ref() is not None)
print("exclude_if model alive:", exclude_if_model_ref() is not None)
```
